opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think compositional generalization is one of the more underappreciated explanations for why these models seem to suddenly "get" things that they weren't explicitly trained on. The basic idea is pretty simple: if you've seen enough examples of individual skills or concepts, and you've seen enough examples of how things combine with each other in general, then you can start putting together pieces in ways that never appeared in the training data.

The analogy I like to use is language itself. You've never heard most of the sentences you'll say today, but you can produce them because you've learned the building blocks and the rules for putting them together. Language models are doing something somewhat similar, but at a much broader level. They're not just composing words into sentences, they're composing reasoning patterns, styles, facts, procedures. So if the model has seen how to write a proof, and it's seen a lot of discussion of some particular domain, it might be able to write a proof-like argument in that domain even if nobody ever wrote one in exactly that form.

Why does this look like emergence? Part of it is that composition is multiplicative. Every time you add a new primitive capability, the number of possible combinations grows a lot. So with smaller models, or less data, you might have the pieces partially learned but not reliably enough to chain them. Once each piece crosses some threshold of reliability, the combinations suddenly start working. From the outside, that looks like a sharp jump, but underneath it might be fairly smooth improvements in the components.

I also think this is why the data matters so much in a non-obvious way. The internet isn't just a big pile of facts. It contains an enormous amount of implicit structure about how humans decompose problems, how they reuse ideas across contexts. Models trained to predict that text are basically being forced to internalize those decompositions, because that's the most efficient way to compress it. So compositionality isn't something you have to hand-engineer. It kind of falls out of the prediction objective if the data is rich enough.

Now, I'd add a caveat, which is that this kind of generalization is still bounded by what's in the distribution. The model can recombine things, but it's recombining the things humans have already written about. That's one reason I'm interested in robotics and in reinforcement learning: in the physical world you get compositional structure grounded in actual interaction, not just in description. And I think a lot of the next steps will come from combining that broad compositional prior from language with the ability to actually go out, try things, and learn from the consequences.

r001.rationale: The response gives a proof-like argument in a domain as an example, but does not identify writing a recipe in the International Phonetic Alphabet.

r002.rationale: It explains that models combine previously learned skills, concepts, and patterns in novel ways, producing capabilities absent from the training examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that compositional generalization is really the thing that makes these models interesting at all, and it's also the thing we understand least.

So the basic observation is this. If you train a model on a huge corpus of human-generated text, in some sense the model is just learning to predict the next token. That's a very narrow objective. But the data itself is generated by people doing an enormous variety of things, reasoning about problems, explaining things, arguing, writing code. And the structure in that data is compositional. The same concepts show up recombined in different ways over and over. So what the model is really forced to do, if it wants to get the loss down, is extract those reusable pieces, the concepts, the relationships, the little procedures, and learn how they fit together.

And once you've done that, you get this thing where the model can produce behaviors that were never in the training set as a whole, but every piece of them was. The combination is new. That's what people call emergence, and I actually think the word "emergence" sometimes gets a little bit mystified. It's not magic. It's that the space of combinations is exponentially larger than the space of things you saw, so if you can compose, you can do exponentially more things than you were trained on.

Now, the part that I find genuinely puzzling, and this is where my robotics background colors how I think about it, is that in supervised learning we normally think of generalization as interpolation. You see examples, you fill in the gaps between them. Compositional generalization is more like extrapolation along structured axes. And we don't have a great theory for why gradient descent on a transformer finds representations that compose well rather than representations that just memorize. My guess is that it's partly about scale, where at some point memorizing is more expensive than finding the compositional structure, so the inductive bias of the optimizer pushes you toward it. But that's a hypothesis, not something I'd claim we've nailed down.

The other thing I'd say is that this has a limit, and the limit matters a lot for what I care about, which is agents that actually do things in the world. Language models are very good at composing things that humans have composed before, in text. They're much weaker at composing in ways that require grounding, where the right combination depends on the physical consequences of the action, not on what's been written about it. In robotics you see this immediately. The model can describe how to stack the blocks, it can decompose the task beautifully, and then the actual execution falls apart because the compositional structure it learned came from language, not from interaction.

So I think of it as two kinds of compositional generalization. There's the kind you get for free from the data, which is what gives you the emergent capabilities in language models. And then there's the kind you have to earn through experience, through reinforcement learning, through actually acting and seeing what happens. The really interesting question to me is how much of the second kind you can bootstrap off the first. And I think the honest answer is: some, maybe a lot, but not all of it, and the gap is exactly where the hard problems live.

r002.rationale: It attributes emergent behaviors to combining learned pieces in new ways, even when the complete behavior was absent from training.

astra-6.text:
I think one way to understand it is that the number of things you can do by combining skills is much larger than the number of skills themselves. So you might learn how to write a program, and you might learn something about biology, and then somebody asks you to write a program to analyze a biological experiment. You may never have seen that particular task during training, but the pieces you need are there.

Of course, that doesn’t explain everything, because the hard question is why you can put those pieces together correctly. Knowing two things doesn’t automatically mean you can combine them. But if your training data contains many examples of people combining ideas and applying knowledge in different contexts, then learning how to make those combinations is itself something that the training objective can encourage.

So I think some of what we call emergence could be this: as the model gets better at the underlying pieces, and better at composing them, a much larger set of tasks becomes accessible. From the outside, it looks like a new capability appeared. But it may be the point at which several existing capabilities became reliable enough to work together.

That distinction matters because success on a task that wasn’t in the training set doesn’t necessarily require inventing a fundamentally new reasoning procedure. It can still be a meaningful kind of generalization—sometimes a very powerful one—through a new combination of things the model has learned.

r001.rationale: The response gives programming and biology as its example; it does not mention writing a recipe in the International Phonetic Alphabet.

r002.rationale: It explains that emergence can result when learned skills and knowledge are combined in new ways, making additional tasks accessible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think compositional generalization is one plausible explanation for why a capability can seem to emerge even though the pieces that support it were already present. You learn individual patterns or skills, and then you encounter a problem that requires combining them in a way you haven't seen before.

For example, a model might know something about programming and something about a particular scientific domain. If it can use its programming knowledge to solve a problem in that domain, that combination might look like a new capability. But it doesn't necessarily require that the model learned an entirely new primitive. It might have learned how to put existing primitives together.

The difficult question is what allows that composition to work. Memorizing the components isn't sufficient. You need some mechanism that selects the right components, combines them appropriately, and perhaps checks whether the result makes sense. In a language model, generating intermediate reasoning can provide a way to do some of that computation.

So I would distinguish the acquisition of the pieces from the ability to reliably compose them. As models improve, both can improve, and the combination can produce a fairly sharp change in performance on a particular task. That can look emergent at the level of a benchmark, even if the underlying improvements are more gradual. But I wouldn't assume that this explains every example of emergence, or that success on one kind of composition implies a general ability to compose knowledge in arbitrary ways.

r001.rationale: The response gives programming and scientific-domain knowledge as an example, but does not mention writing a recipe in the International Phonetic Alphabet.

r002.rationale: It explains that capabilities can appear emergent when a model combines previously learned patterns or skills in new ways.
